newsitem.title: FRANCE: France probes new British rent-to-own shop.
newsitem.headline: France probes new British rent-to-own shop.

text.p: France launched an inquiry on Sunday into British rent-to-own chain Crazy George's amid charges by the opposition Socialist Party that a new shop would trap the poor into over-paying for goods like sofas and stereos.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said he had asked the official consumer watchdog to see whether Crazy George's, owned by electronics giant Thorn Plc, complied with consumer protection laws.

Crazy George's opened its first French outlet on Saturday in Bobigny, a northern Paris suburb, as part of a European expansion. The chain has 45 shops in Britain, modelled on a successful U.S. formula.
"The authorities should protect consumers and not let them be abused by misleading behaviour or publicity," Arthuis said on Sunday.

"If someone tells you you're the owner of a fridge after paying 20 francs ($4) and the contract is not a sales contract but a rental contract with a purchase option, then the advertising is clearly deceitful," he told TF1 television.
"These are shops for poor people where the poor will be paying twice what the rich pay," Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin said.
"It's a way of exploiting poverty," he said on Saturday night. "This is something really crazy and absurd."

Among Crazy George's offers in France, for instance, is a freezer, at 85 francs ($17) a week. Costing 5,987 francs ($1,170) to buy outright, it ends up costing 13,260 francs ($2,600) after three years' rental.
Goods can be returned at any time and Crazy George's says the so-called New Buy Scheme enables people with little income to obtain household goods without getting into debt.
But Jospin's charges seemed to touch a raw nerve in France, which is grappling with record unemployment of 12.6 percent and persistent gloom about the economy and wide social inequalities.

Several other charities for aiding the poor also criticised the shop. "Crazy George's is just a decoy, hidden behind an attractive slogan," Denis Vienot, head of the Roman Catholic relief group Caritas France, told the daily France Soir.
